summary: NETCONF is a protocol for installing, changing and deleting the configuration of network devices. Messages and configuration data are encoded in XML, and operations are carried as simple remote procedure calls. It was replaced by RFC 6241.

eli5.summary: A router has a long settings list. NETCONF is a polite, standard way for a computer to ask the router to change its settings, so every brand of router understands the same request.

questions: how to configure network devices with xml
how do you configure devices with netconf
subtitle: A standard way to configure network devices with XML-based messages.

tldr.problem: Network device configuration is often vendor-specific and cumbersome. Administrators need a unified, standardized protocol for installing, modifying and deleting configurations across different devices.
tldr.mechanism: NETCONF provides a layered protocol that uses XML to encode configuration data and remote procedure calls. Clients send RPC requests over secure, persistent connections to devices acting as servers, which respond with RPC replies containing results or errors.
tldr.outcome: Devices can expose configuration management via a formal API, and managers can programmatically configure multiple devices in a consistent way. It was obsoleted by RFC 6241, which adds features like YANG data modeling.

today: RFC 4741 was obsoleted by RFC 6241, which updates NETCONF to version 1.1 and adds support for the YANG data modeling language, allowing standard definitions of configuration schemas that all implementations can rely on.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
NETCONF is the Network Configuration Protocol, designed to install, manipulate and delete configurations on network devices. It uses XML for both configuration data and protocol messages, with operations realized as remote procedure calls (RPCs).

A key aspect of NETCONF is that it lets the protocol closely mirror the device's native functionality, reducing implementation costs and allowing timely access to new features. Devices advertise capabilities to clients—sets of protocol extensions like support for candidate configuration datastores or atomic commits. This allows clients to adjust their behavior based on what the device supports.
sections.eli5: A network device tells a client (like a configuration tool) what settings it can change and how. The client then sends properly-formatted requests and the device replies with either success or an error explaining what went wrong.

sections.title: Four-Layer Architecture
sections.content: NETCONF is conceptually organized into four layers. The transport layer (Layer 1) carries messages over a protocol like SSH or BEEP, providing authentication, integrity and confidentiality. The RPC layer (Layer 2) provides transport-independent framing of requests and responses using <rpc> and <rpc-reply> elements. The operations layer (Layer 3) defines base operations like <get-config>, <edit-config>, and <lock>, invoked as RPC methods. The content layer (Layer 4) is outside NETCONF's scope and depends on device-specific data models.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mailbox system: the transport layer is the physical mailbox and postal service; the RPC layer is the envelope format; the operations layer is the list of things you can ask for (like 'get this config'); and the content layer is what's actually in the envelope.

sections.title: RPC Messages and Replies
sections.content:
Every NETCONF request is wrapped in an <rpc> element with a mandatory message-id attribute. The RPC name and parameters are encoded as child elements inside the <rpc>. For example, a <get-config> operation includes a <source> element specifying which datastore to retrieve.

Servers respond with <rpc-reply> elements containing the same message-id to match requests to replies. Success responses include an <ok> element or a <data> element with results. Errors are returned as <rpc-error> elements, which specify the error type (transport, rpc, protocol or application), a tag, severity, and optionally a message and error-specific content.
sections.eli5: Every request has a numbered envelope so you can match replies to the right request. Success or failure is marked clearly, and errors include a reason so you know what went wrong.

sections.title: Protocol Operations
sections.content:
NETCONF defines eight base operations. <get-config> retrieves configuration data from a named datastore (like <running>) with optional filtering. <edit-config> loads configuration into a target datastore with operations like merge, replace, create or delete. <copy-config> duplicates an entire configuration datastore. <delete-config> removes a datastore (not the running one).

<lock> acquires an exclusive lock on a datastore to prevent other sessions from modifying it. <unlock> releases a lock. <get> retrieves both configuration and state (read-only) data. <close-session> gracefully terminates a session, releasing locks and resources. <kill-session> forcefully terminates another session.

NETCONF defines only one configuration datastore in the base protocol: <running>, the active configuration. Optional capabilities add <candidate> (a work area) and <startup> (loaded on boot) datastores.
sections.eli5: NETCONF lets you read configuration, change it, copy it, delete it, lock it so others can't touch it, and close the connection. Think of it as saving a file, editing it, backing it up, and locking it when you're working on it.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
NETCONF separates configuration data (writable information needed to reach a desired state) from state data (read-only status and statistics). This separation allows cleaner comparisons and prevents accidents like trying to write to read-only fields. The <get-config> operation retrieves only configuration, while <get> retrieves both.

Subtree filtering allows clients to request only parts of the configuration using XML element matching. Filters can select entire subtrees, specific leaf elements, or elements matching content values.

Capabilities are extensibility features identified by URIs. Servers advertise capabilities during session setup via a <hello> message. Base capabilities include support for writable-running, candidate configuration, confirmed commits (where a change is automatically rolled back unless confirmed), validation before applying changes, rollback on error, distinct startup configurations, URL sources for configuration, and XPath filtering. New capabilities can be defined without disturbing existing implementations.
sections.eli5: Configuration is the stuff you can change; state is the stuff you can only read. Filters let you ask for just what you want instead of everything. And devices tell you upfront what fancy features they support so you know what you can do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Configuration data is inherently sensitive, often containing passwords, usernames, and topological information. NETCONF requires that all connections be secure, relying on transport protocols like SSH to provide authentication, integrity and confidentiality. The protocol does not define authorization; that is left to implementers to tie to data models or other schemes.

Authorization enforcement is critical when multiple sessions access the same device. For example, a user lacking permission to change an IP address must not be able to commit a candidate configuration containing such a change, even if another user made the change. Similarly, the <lock> operation locks the entire configuration, potentially allowing access to data a principal might not normally see, so administrative trust is required. Two mitigation approaches are defined: programmatically killing an offending NETCONF session if you know its ID, or using the device's native user interface to break the lock.
sections.eli5: Network configuration is sensitive stuff like passwords and network layout. All communication must be encrypted and authenticated. Devices need to carefully check that you're allowed to make the changes you're asking for.
